answers.plain:
Here's a speech of about 2 minutes (roughly 280 words at a relaxed pace):

---

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm [your name], and I had the privilege of working alongside Gloria.

Thirty-one years. Think about that. Gloria started teaching sixth grade science here when some of today's parents were sixth graders. She has taught the children, and in some cases the children's children, why volcanoes erupt, how plants grow, and why you should never, ever taste the experiment.

And Gloria didn't just teach science. She *lived* it. She started the robotics club, which means that for years this school has had children building small machines that roll, grab, and occasionally drive straight into the principal's office. Gloria never panicked. She just said, "Well, that's data."

Then there's the school garden. Gloria looked at a patch of dirt and saw tomatoes, sunflowers, and a classroom with no walls. Now, I'll be honest: I've seen sixth graders refuse to eat vegetables from a cafeteria tray. But hand them a carrot they pulled out of the ground themselves, and suddenly they're gourmet critics. That's Gloria's magic. She makes curious people out of kids who didn't know they were curious.

What I'll remember most is how she treated every question as a good one, even the one about whether a robot could do your homework. (Her answer: "Sure, if you build it. Then you've done your homework.")

Gloria, you've planted something here that will keep growing long after today. Every student who ever fixed a robot, or knelt in the dirt to plant a seed, carries a little of you with them.

So enjoy your retirement. You've earned the rest, and we promise to water the garden.

Everyone, please raise your glass.

**To Gloria: you taught us that the best discoveries start with a question, and the best lives keep growing. Cheers!**

---

A few quick tips:
- Pause after the "taste the experiment" and "that's data" lines to let the laughs land.
- If you have a real anecdote, like a specific robot mishap or a garden story, swap it in for the principal's office joke. Personal details always land best.
- If you'd like it shorter or funnier, or want me to add a specific memory, tell me and I'll adjust.
answers.nudge:
# Gloria's Retirement Toast (about 2 minutes)

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm [name], and I have the honor of working with Gloria. Tonight I get to roast her gently, because she's holding a cupcake and can't reach me.

Gloria taught 6th grade science here for 31 years. Do the math on that. She has spent roughly 5,600 school weeks with eleven-year-olds, and she did it *on purpose*, again and again. That isn't a career. That's a long-running experiment in human endurance, and the results are in: she's a hero.

She taught thousands of kids that the world is full of questions worth asking. She also taught them that "I don't know, let's find out" is one of the most powerful sentences in the English language. Then she let them find out, which sometimes meant a smell in the hallway. We don't talk about the volcano year. [Swap in your own favorite Gloria story here.]

Then she started the robotics club. Gloria looked at a room of sixth graders and thought, "Let's give them motors and a deadline." Somehow it worked. Kids who thought they were just "not science people" went home having built something that *moved*, because they made it move. Some of those robots even did what they were told, which is more than I can say for the kids.

And the garden. She took a patch of dirt and turned it into a place where kids learned that food doesn't start at the store, and that patience is a skill. [Mention a detail: the tomatoes, the sunflowers, the bench.] That garden will keep growing long after today.

That's really her whole story. Gloria plants things: curiosity, confidence, actual tomatoes. Then she steps back and lets them grow.

So please raise your glass.

**Gloria, you are the proof that great teachers are never really done. They just go on to grow in other gardens. To Gloria!**

---

**Delivery notes**
- **Timing:** This runs about 2 minutes at a relaxed pace, around 330 words. If you're nervous or the room laughs a lot, cut the "5,600 school weeks" line.
- **Personalize:** The two bracketed spots matter most. One real, specific anecdote, like a particular student, a failed experiment, or something she always says, will beat any of my jokes. Keep each to one or two sentences.
- **Check the math:** 31 years × about 36 school weeks is roughly 1,100 weeks, not 5,600. I got that wrong in the draft, so use "over a thousand school weeks" instead.
- **Pause:** Wait a beat before the last line. Raise your glass at "So please raise your glass" and say the closing line as people lift theirs.

If you tell me one or two real Gloria stories, I'll work them in and tighten it to your exact time.
answers.skill:
Good evening, everyone. I'm [your name], and I have a confession. I have worked down the hall from Gloria for [number] years, and I still don't know how a plant and a robot can both take over a classroom.

But Gloria managed it. Every time.

Here's what I figured out. A robot and a garden are the same job. You build something. You tend it. It doesn't work. You try again.

Gloria taught sixth grade science for 31 years. That's a lot of volcanoes. A lot of bean sprouts in paper cups. A lot of kids saying, "It's broken," and Gloria saying, "Okay. What do we try next?"

I've seen that happen with a robot that drove in circles. I've seen it with tomatoes that [funny garden mishap]. Same calm face. Same answer. Try again.

You started the robotics club. You built the school garden. You made things that needed patience, and then you handed that patience to eleven-year-olds. That's the hard part.

Now here's where I stop joking. Almost.

Think about sixth grade. Kids are awkward. They're growing too fast and feel sure they're doing it wrong. And for 31 years, Gloria gave them a place where being wrong was just step one.

Some of them [a specific memory only you'd know] are grown now. Some are probably fixing real machines and growing real food. Some just know that a mistake isn't the end.

That's what you built. Not just a club. Not just a garden. People who keep going.

So Gloria, enjoy the quiet. Sleep past the bell. And if something breaks, you're allowed to let someone else fix it.

Everyone, please raise a glass.

To Gloria: you built it, you tended it, you tried again, and look what grew.
